explanations.battle-of-breitenfeld-1631--battle-of-th: The Alte Veste article makes Breitenfeld one of the two reasons Wallenstein was in the field to be met at all: "The earlier successes of Gustavus Adolphus over General Tilly, particularly at Breitenfeld, followed by Tilly's death during the Battle of Rain, forced Holy Roman Emperor Ferdinand II to recall Albrecht von Wallenstein into military service from retirement." The paragraph carries no citation of its own, so Wikipedia is the only author named and the confidence stays probable.
explanations.battle-of-fort-albany--battle-of-fort-al: The 1693 article says what there was to recapture and how it came to be French: "The fort, captured by a French expedition in 1686 and held by them in a battle the next year, was briefly defended by five Frenchmen, who then abandoned the fort and its stockpile of furs to a four-ship English fleet commanded by James Knight." The battle in which the French held it is the one this atlas records as `battle-of-fort-albany`, whose own article at revision 1366220638 opens "The 1688 Battle of Fort Albany was one of the Anglo-French conflicts on Hudson Bay" and describes the same fight over the same garrison. **The two articles disagree about its year** — the 1693 one says the year after 1686 and the other says 1688 — and the item's own P580 is September 1688, which is what this record carries; nothing was changed to make them agree. The recapture presupposes the holding either way, which is what this edge says. Neither sentence is footnoted to any work Wikipedia names, so Wikipedia is the only author and the confidence stays probable.
explanations.battle-of-lutzen-1632--battle-of-oldendo: The Oldendorf article dates its own campaign from the death at Lützen: "After Gustavus Adolphus was killed in November 1632, the Duke of Brunswick was appointed local Swedish commander. The 1633 campaign focused on securing the supply route stretching from Bremen on the coast south along the River Weser." The siege of Hamelin that Oldendorf was fought to relieve is the first move of that campaign. The sentence carries the article's own citation to Guthrie (2003), p. 238, which is the second author named here.
explanations.battle-of-mata-redonda--campaign-of-port: The campaign's own article puts the expedition beaten at Mata Redonda at the head of its background: John Maurice "was also sent for another reason since, Don Luis de Rojas y Borgia arrived in Brazil Upon his arrival, he disembarked his troops at Jaragua and initiated guerrilla warfare against the opposing forces. This involved attacks on farms and plantations. These actions were primarily carried out from the captaincy of Porto Calvo. At one point, a proposal was put forth by Von Schoppe to undertake a more aggressive approach by attacking and destroying the enemy bases. Despite initial reservations, this proposal was eventually accepted. As a result, a decision was made to shift from a defensive stance of protecting farms and plantations to an offensive strategy." Rojas y Borja's armada is what the Battle of Mata Redonda is the record of — its own article has him killed there on 18 January 1636 — and Marley 2008 runs the two consecutively, the battle at p. 191 and the campaign at p. 192. `precondition-of` and not `caused`: the article gives the campaign two reasons, Nassau's appointment and his own ambition being the other, so the force left at Porto Calvo is what the 1637 offensive was aimed at rather than what set it off.
explanations.battle-of-nordlingen-1634--battle-of-wit: The Wittstock article opens its background with Nördlingen: "After the Swedish defeat at Nördlingen in 1634, many protestant princes of the Holy Roman Empire lost faith in their alliance with Sweden and reconciled with the emperor. In May 1635, the Elector of Saxony agreed to the Peace of Prague with Emperor Ferdinand II… In northern Germany, a corps of the Habsburg Imperial army and the Saxon army fought against the last significant Swedish forces." The Saxon army Banér and Leslie met at Wittstock is on the Imperial side because of what Nördlingen did to the alliance. The paragraph carries no citation of its own, so Wikipedia is the only author named.
explanations.battle-of-nordlingen-1634--siege-of-brei: The Breisach article traces the besieger's independent command to his defeat at Nördlingen: "Bernard of Saxe-Weimar aspired to acquire his own territory in the Holy Roman Empire. After his defeat as Swedish commander at Nördlingen in 1634, he commanded… the former troops of the Protestant Heilbronn League. A treaty with France brought him reinforcements, pay and provisions. In 1637, he went onto the offensive against Breisach, a potential capital for his desired territory." The paragraph is cited to Ackermann (2023), p. 215, which is the second author named here.
explanations.battle-of-port-royal-1690--battle-of-que: The Quebec article says so in one sentence: "Following the capture of Port Royal in Acadia, during King William's War, the New Englanders hoped to seize Quebec City itself, the capital of New France." The capture in May is what put the capital within reach and is what the expedition of October was raised on; the article states the sequence as a reason and not only as an order, and the edge says that and no more. The sentence is not footnoted to any work Wikipedia names, so Wikipedia is the only author and the confidence stays probable.
explanations.battle-of-rain--battle-of-the-alte-veste: The same sentence names Rain as the other half of the reason: "particularly at Breitenfeld, followed by Tilly's death during the Battle of Rain, forced Holy Roman Emperor Ferdinand II to recall Albrecht von Wallenstein into military service from retirement." The section adds the march that followed: "In spring of 1632, Gustavus Adolphus had handed the Habsburg Emperor, Ferdinand II, a major defeat at Rain… He subsequently occupied Nuremberg, encamping his army outside of the city." Uncited in the article, so probable.
explanations.battle-of-rio-bueno-1654--mapuche-uprisi: The uprising's own article puts the two in one sequence and says which way it runs: "In 1654 a large slave-hunting expedition ended in a complete disaster at the Battle of Río Bueno. This setback did not stop the Spanish who under the leadership of Salazar organized a new expedition the summer of 1655." It then has the Mapuche rising as that expedition was being prepared — "As the slave raiding expedition of 1655 was being prepared indios amigos begun to express unease" — and Salazar beginning his campaign on 6 February with the attacks following on 14 February. Precondition-of and not caused: the article is explicit that the defeat did not stop the raiding, so the battle is a step on the way to the expedition the rising answered and not the thing that brought the rising about.
explanations.battle-of-the-alte-veste--battle-of-lutz: The article puts Lützen among the Alte Veste's own results: "Several weeks later, lack of supplies led Wallenstein to break camp and move north, allowing the Swedes out of Nuremberg. The two armies met again two months later at the Battle of Lützen, where Gustavus was killed," and before it: "The immediate result of the Nuremberg campaign allowed the Habsburgs to advance into Saxony." The stalemate at Nuremberg is what sent Wallenstein into Saxony, which is the ground Lützen was fought over. Uncited in the article, so probable.
explanations.battle-of-zusmarshausen--battle-of-pragu: The Zusmarshausen article puts the raid on Prague among the campaign's own consequences: "However, the Swedes took advantage of the weakened defences in Bohemia; a second Swedish army under Königsmarck took the castle and the Malá Strana district of Prague by surprise on 25 July. Their following siege of the Old and the New Town at the other side of the Vltava river continued even after the final conclusion of the negotiations…" The armies drawn into Bavaria after Zusmarshausen are the defences Bohemia lacked. The paragraph carries the article's own citation to Wilson, Europe’s Tragedy, Penguin 2010 printing, pp. 744-747, which is the second author named here.
explanations.bohemian-revolt--siege-of-pilsen--enable: The siege’s own article puts the two in that order and names the army: “The Siege of Pilsen, 19 September to 21 November 1618, was the first significant action of the Thirty Years’ War. Following the Bohemian Revolt, a Bohemian army under Ernst von Mansfeld captured Plzeň.” The army that took the city is the revolt’s own, which is why this is `enabled` rather than `caused`: the article says the revolt put that force in the field, not that it decided the siege. `probable`, on one lead, and rule 22 refuses `consensus` on a Wikipedia citation.
explanations.bohemian-revolt--thirty-years-war--cause: The revolt’s own article states it in the first sentence: it was “an uprising of the Bohemian estates against the rule of the Habsburg dynasty that began the Thirty Years’ War”. The same lead says the defeat at White Mountain “expanded the scope of the Thirty Years’ War by drawing Denmark and Sweden into it”, so the article treats the revolt as the thing the war grew out of and not merely as its first episode. The atlas already types a war’s opening action this way — Operation Rosary and the Falklands War, the Moncada attack and the Cuban Revolution — and this is that shape. It stays `probable`: one encyclopaedia lead reporting where the consensus sits is not a work arguing it, and rule 22 would refuse `consensus` on a Wikipedia citation in any case. That the revolt is also filed as part of the war is a separate statement; `parent` does not enter the adjacency, so the argument has to be made as an edge or not at all.
explanations.capture-of-bahia--campaign-of-porto-calv: The Campaign of Porto Calvo article, § Background, puts the campaign at the end of a sequence it starts at Bahia: "the year 1624 saw the Dutch fleet arriving off the coast of Salvador, where a swift invasion ensued, resulting in the city’s capture within a remarkably brief span of 24 hours. This marked an acceleration of their territorial expansion in Brazil", and then, of the campaign itself, that John Maurice, governor from 1636, "spearheaded multiple far-reaching expeditions aimed at further territorial growth and consolidation". `enabled` is the type the article’s own wording carries: the 1624 capture is what it says the expansion accelerated from, thirteen years before this campaign, and not a cause of this campaign in particular. Probable: Wikipedia alone, at two revisions. The article attributes the passage to Clemmy Manzo, The Rough Guide to Brazil (2014) and to Erik Odegard, Patronage, Patrimonialism, and Governors’ Careers in the Dutch Chartered Companies, 1630–1681 (2022), pp. 60–62 — works Wikipedia itself cites, which A2 would allow as a second author, and neither was read here, so the edge stays probable.
explanations.capture-of-bahia--dutch-brazil-1630-1654: The 1624 seizure of Salvador was the West India Company's first attempt on Brazil, and the colony of 1630 was the second one. The Dutch Brazil article, at revision 1375595876, puts both in the same design: "As part of the Groot Desseyn plan, admiral Jacob Willekens led a GWC force to Salvador in December 1623, which was then the capital of Brazil and the center of a captaincy famous for its sugarcane", and then, of the funds Piet Heyn took at Matanzas Bay in 1628, that they "provided the GWC the funds for another attempt to conquer Brazil at Pernambuco" — another attempt is an attempt after the first. The Capture of Bahia article names the same plan. `precondition-of` and not `caused`: the article makes the 1630 conquest the second try of one Company design, and does not say the first try brought the second about.
explanations.capture-of-bahia--recapture-of-bahia--re: The Capture of Bahia article closes its lead on the answer this edge names: "Although the Dutch intentions were reported to the Spanish, no preventive counter-action was taken until the Recapture of Bahia in 1625." The Recapture article opens with the same thing said from the other side: "The recapture of Bahia was a Spanish–Portuguese military expedition in 1625 to retake the city of Bahia in Brazil from the forces of the Dutch West India Company (WIC)." An expedition mounted to retake a city taken the year before is a reaction to the taking and not a consequence of it, so `reacted-to` and not `caused`. Probable, because both articles are read at one revision each and neither names a historian for the reading.
explanations.dutch-brazil-1630-1654--battle-of-abrolh: The Abrolhos article puts the Dutch fleet where the Dutch colony had put it: Oquendo "carried reinforcements to Paraíba, Pernambuco, and Bahia", and "Once the Dutch learned of his coming, their fleet in Pernambuco, led by admiral Adrian Pater, sailed to intercept the Spanish convoy." A Dutch fleet of thirty-three ships lying at Pernambuco in 1631 is what the capture of 1630 left there, and the battle is the convoy meeting it. `precondition-of`: the colony is the state of affairs the battle begins from, and the article says the fleet sailed because Oquendo was coming and not because of anything the colony did. Probable: Wikipedia alone, and the article's own account of both ends.
explanations.dutch-brazil-1630-1654--conquest-of-para: The Conquest of Paraíba article, § Details, opens the account of the expedition with the conquest that preceded it: "After conquering Recife, Lichthart decided to set sail for Paraíba. In December, Lichthart led an expedition towards Paraíba with a fleet comprising 21 ships and 11 yachts". The Dutch hold on Recife is what this atlas carries as `dutch-brazil-1630-1654`, whose own summary dates it from 1630 with "the West India Company’s headquarters and the capital Mauritsstad at Recife"; the fleet that took Paraíba sailed from there and was the colony’s. `precondition-of` and not `caused`: the article states what the expedition set out from and not that holding Recife made the conquest follow. Probable: Wikipedia alone, at two revisions.
explanations.dutch-brazil-1630-1654--siege-of-salvado: The siege article names the colony as the thing that mounted it: "The governor of the Dutch colony in Brazil, John Maurice, Prince of Nassau-Siegen, commanding the army of the Dutch West India Company, with vastly superior forces and a supporting fleet under Johan van der Mast, put the city of Salvador under siege." The 1640 action's article calls the same event "John Maurits of Nassau's attack over Bahia". `enabled`: the colony and its army are what made a march on Salvador possible from Pernambuco, and neither article says the colony's existence obliged it. Probable: Wikipedia alone, at two revisions.
explanations.dutch-brazil-1630-1654--the-caribbean-su: This is the edge that makes the two chains one picture, and it is a transfer of a technique, a people and a supply chain rather than a resemblance. The cane that transformed Barbados came from Dutch Brazil in 1640; Colonel James Drax went to Pernambuco that year and bought a triple-roller mill and a set of copper cauldrons; the Sephardic families who had left Iberia for Dutch Brazil were, in the cited account, instrumental in the early success of the Barbadian industry; and Dutch traders supplied the equipment, the financing, the enslaved Africans and the shipping to Europe. What the West India Company had built at Recife it lost by 1654, and it had already been carried north.
explanations.dutch-portuguese-war--dutch-brazil-1630-: Dutch Brazil was the American theatre of this war and not an enterprise beside it. The war's article, at revision 1374150566, describes a conflict in which "the Dutch companies and fleet" were "invading Portuguese colonies in the Americas, Africa, and the East Indies"; the Dutch Brazil article dates the American half of that to the fleet of sixty-five ships under Hendrick Corneliszoon Loncq, which "gained control of Olinda by 16 February 1630, and Recife (the capital of Pernambuco) and António Vaz by March 3". `enabled` rather than `caused`: the war is what made a Company fleet in Brazilian waters possible, and the colony is one of the things that possibility was spent on. The atlas also files the colony under the war as a part of it; `parent` does not enter the adjacency, so the causal reading is written here or nowhere.
explanations.english-settlement-of-barbados-1627--the: The first ship to the settlement carried six enslaved Africans among sixty-odd settlers, and about forty enslaved Taíno were brought from Guyana to plant. The scale is the whole difference from what came after: before 1650 more than three quarters of the islands’ population was of European descent, and by 1680 the median Barbadian estate held sixty enslaved people. The colony is where the traffic landed; it is not why it grew.

Thirteen years separate the landing at Holetown from the cane that changed everything, and in those thirteen years Barbados was a tobacco colony of tenants working for a London merchant. That is the point of keeping the two records apart rather than writing one: the settlement is not the sugar revolution and did not contain it in embryo. What it supplied was an English island with cleared ground, a population and a proprietor — the thing Drax could bring a mill back to in 1640.
explanations.first-battle-of-guararapes--second-battl: The Second Battle of Guararapes article calls itself "the second and decisive battle in the Insurrection of Pernambuco", takes the First Battle as its § Background — "{{Main|First Battle of Guararapes}}" — and says there, in so many words, what the second answered: "Facing an uprising by the Portuguese planters in Dutch Brazil and having concluded a Peace Treaty with the Spanish in 1647, the Dutch sent an expeditionary force to Brazil, consisting of 41 ships with 6000 men. This expeditionary force arrived late in Recife (Mauritsstad) and faced numerous problems. In April 1648, the Portuguese routed the expeditionary force at the First Battle of Guararapes, fought outside Recife." The same force fought again ten months later on the same ground. `precondition-of` rather than `caused`: the article makes the first battle the state of affairs the second begins from, and does not say the first brought the second about. Probable: Wikipedia alone, at two revisions.
explanations.iroquois-war-1609--battle-of-sorel--prec: The Sorel article reads the 1609 fight as what put Champlain and the Mohawk on opposite sides for good: "The first deliberate battle in 1609 was fought at Champlain's initiative. Champlain deliberately went along with a war party down Lake Champlain. Furthermore, this battle created 150 years of mistrust that poisoned any chances that French-Iroquois alliances would be durable and long lived." The second battle is the first one continued a year later, with the same alliance and the same arquebuses. Wikipedia is the only author named, so probable.
explanations.lachine-massacre--battle-of-the-lake-of-: The article opens on the connection: "The battle occurred in response to the Lachine massacre of August 1689. In October, Governor General of New France, the Marquis de Denonville dispatched a scouting party of 28 coureur des bois … to search for Haudenosaunee warriors that posed a threat to residents on the Island of Montreal." The scouting party is what the massacre produced; the skirmish is what the party found. Wikipedia is the only author named, so probable.
explanations.lachine-massacre--schenectady-massacre--: The Schenectady article says so in one sentence: "The French raid was in retaliation for the Lachine massacre, an attack by Haudenosaunee forces on a village in New France." Read in this direction the edge says what the article supports and no more — the February raid followed the August one and was made as an answer to it. The article carries citations of its own but the sentence is not footnoted to any work Wikipedia names, so Wikipedia is the only author here and the confidence stays probable.
explanations.mohawk-valley-raid--battle-of-wilton-new: The raid article describes the battle as what the raid ran into on its way home: "The raiders, burdened with their prisoners, were followed by a rapidly deployed English-Iroquois force led by Major Pieter Schuyler. The two forces engaged in skirmishing a few days after the raid. Because of the pursuit, the raiders were forced to release most of their prisoners." The two records are two ends of one winter: the raid on the three castles, and the running fight of the retreat. Wikipedia is the only author named, so probable.
explanations.mohawk-valley-raid--great-peace-of-montr: The article states the consequence in its own words: "The Mohawk were seriously weakened as a military force within the Iroquois league, and the raid's effects contributed to the 1701 peace negotiated between the Iroquois, French, and many other tribes." Precondition-of and not caused: the article says the raid contributed to the peace, not that it brought it about, and nine years and several other actions stand between them. Wikipedia is the only author named, so probable.
explanations.peace-of-prague-1635--battle-of-chemnitz: The Chemnitz article begins its background with the same defection: "The former Swedish ally Saxony defected in the Peace of Prague (1635) to Emperor Ferdinand II." The detachment Banér destroyed at Chemnitz was a combined Saxon and Imperial one, and the article gives the Peace as the reason Saxony was on that side. The paragraph carries no citation of its own, so Wikipedia is the only author named.
explanations.peace-of-prague-1635--battle-of-wittstoc: The same paragraph names the Peace itself as the step between Nördlingen and the field: "In May 1635, the Elector of Saxony agreed to the Peace of Prague with Emperor Ferdinand II… In northern Germany, a corps of the Habsburg Imperial army and the Saxon army fought against the last significant Swedish forces." Wittstock was fought by a combined Imperial-Saxon army, which is the army the Peace of Prague made. Uncited in the article, so probable.
explanations.portuguese-conquest-of-maricay--capture-: The article's own lead places it: "The Portuguese Conquest of Maricay was a series of battles between the Portuguese Empire under the Iberian Union and the Dutch Republic, taking place in 1623 in the trading post of Maricay, now Gurupá. Taking place one year before the Capture of Bahia, the battle is one of the events leading to thirty years of war between the Portuguese and Dutch in Brazil." `precondition-of` and not `caused`: the article calls it one of the events leading to the war, which is a place in a sequence and not a cause of the particular invasion of Salvador. The atlas holds that invasion as `capture-of-bahia`, and this edge is the sequence the lead states and nothing beyond it. **No work is cited on that sentence**, so this edge has one source where M72 asks for two, and it stays `probable` for that reason as well as for the claim's own shape.
explanations.saint-domingue-and-the-french-sugar-colo: The revolution is the colony’s own structure coming apart. Ogé’s revolt of free men of colour in 1790 and the citizenship granted them in May 1791 set them against the slave owners and destabilised the colony; the rising of 21 August 1791 came out of that. Saint-Domingue was the most thoroughly enslaved place in the Caribbean and the richest, and the two facts are the same fact; what rose in 1791 was the majority the sugar economy had assembled.
explanations.schenectady-massacre--battle-of-wilton-n: The Wilton article makes the 1690 raid the reason the 1693 one could be found at all: "In sixteen days they reached the Mohawk, led by a guide captured in the Schenectady Massacre, Jan Baptiste Van Eps." The same man then undid it — "Van Eps had escaped before the attacks and made his way to Schenectady, where he alerted the inhabitants to the French attack" — which is how Schuyler came to be on the retreat road. Enabled and not caused: Schenectady did not decide that the Mohawk castles would be attacked, it supplied the man who led the way there. Wikipedia is the only author named, so probable.
explanations.siege-of-pemaquid-1689--battle-of-falmou: The Pemaquid article states what the fall of the fort did to the frontier: "The fall of Pemaquid was a significant setback to the English. It pushed the frontier back to Casco (Falmouth), Maine." Falmouth is where the next year's attack fell, and the article makes the loss of the easternmost outpost the reason it was exposed. The sentences are not footnoted to any work Wikipedia names, so the confidence stays probable.
explanations.siege-of-pemaquid-1696--raid-on-chignect: The Chignecto article says so in one sentence: "The raid was in retaliation for the French and Indian Siege of Pemaquid (1696) at present day Bristol, Maine." It is the same answer the Fort Nashwaak siege was, by the same New England force under Church a month earlier, and the article states the reason rather than only the order. The sentence is not footnoted to any work Wikipedia names, so the confidence stays probable.
explanations.siege-of-pemaquid-1696--siege-of-fort-na: The Fort Nashwaak article says so in one sentence: "The siege was in retaliation for the French and Indian Siege of Pemaquid (1696) in the English Province of Massachusetts Bay." Two months separate them and the article gives the first as the reason for the second, which is what reacted-to is for. The sentence is not footnoted to any work Wikipedia names, so the confidence stays probable.
explanations.siege-of-salvador-1638--action-of-12-17-: The 1640 action's § Background has the failed siege in it and then the expedition: the reinforcements landed in 1635 "greatly contributed to the defeat of John Maurits of Nassau's attack over Bahia", and "Another expedition was planned… to retake the Dutch base of Pernambuco", whose command the Count of Torre took and which sailed with 41 ships and 5,000 soldiers into the action of January 1640. The siege article is the other end: the defenders "managed to resist the Dutch attacks until they gave up taking the city and withdrew". `precondition-of`: holding Bahia in 1638 is the position the 1640 fleet sailed from, and the article stops short of saying the defence brought the expedition about — it says the expedition was planned on Hoces's arrival, before the siege. That gap is why the type is not `caused`. Probable: Wikipedia alone, at two revisions.
explanations.siege-of-stralsund-1628--battle-of-wolga: The Wolgast article says why Wallenstein was in front of Wolgast at all: "Christian IV then awaited Wallenstein, who withdrew from the siege of Stralsund and was heading east to face the Danish force." The battle is the one Wallenstein could fight once Stralsund had held and released his army; the sentence carries the article's own citation to Heckel (1983), p. 143, which is the second author named here.
explanations.the-atlantic-slave-trade-to-the-caribbea: A hundred and fifty years, and the weakest type. The traffic did not organise the rising and nothing about it made a successful revolution likely — the cited account calls it the only slave rebellion known to have founded a state free of slavery and ruled by former captives, which is a statement about how rarely this happened. What the traffic supplied was the demographic fact the revolution was made out of: an enslaved majority, overwhelmingly African-born, in a colony held by a small white population.

A separate claim from the one above and worth keeping separate. That edge says the islands created the demand; this one says the traffic already existed, in Dutch and Portuguese hands — Dutch traders were supplying Barbados with its enslaved labour as well as its equipment and its credit — and that a monopoly company granted by the crown was how England moved to carry its own. A monopoly is a claim on an existing trade, not the invention of one.

France got the western third of Hispaniola recognised at Ryswick in 1697 and made it the richest sugar colony in the Caribbean, which it could do because the Atlantic traffic was by then a going concern that a new colony could buy into rather than build. `enabled` and not `caused`: the traffic did not make France take Saint-Domingue, and the French had been on Tortuga and the western coast for decades before. What it made possible was the speed and the scale.

What struck in Jamaica at Christmas 1831 was the population the traffic had assembled: by the eighteenth century the sugar islands held three enslaved Africans for every planter, and the estates had grown from smallholdings into units of sixty and more. The weak type is right here. The traffic did not organise the strike — a Baptist minister did — and the atlas should not take the agency of the people who withdrew their labour and hand it to the thing that had been done to them. What it supplied is the demographic ground.

The most contested link either chain touches, and the reason `disputed` exists in this schema. The thesis is Eric Williams’s in Capitalism and Slavery (1944), stated by Carrington as: the slave trade and the sugar industry based on slavery led to the formation of capital in England which helped finance the Industrial Revolution. The plantations supplied 80 to 90 per cent of the sugar consumed in western Europe and Barbados alone out-traded every other English colony combined by 1660, so there is no argument about whether the profits were large; the argument is about what they did. The atlas marks the link rather than asserting it, and a reader who opens this edge gets the disagreement rather than a line drawn confidently through it.

The Cuban boom is the last chapter of the traffic this chain is centred on and not a new thing: Cuba kept slavery until October 1886, half a century after the British islands and two years before Brazil, and it kept importing while it could. `enabled` rather than `caused`, because the boom’s occasion was Haiti and its market was North American; what the traffic supplied was the only labour force the Cuban planters intended to use.
explanations.the-brazilian-gold-cycle--the-british-in: The flow is not in doubt and the mechanism is on the record. Eight hundred tonnes of gold were shipped officially from Minas to Portugal over the eighteenth century, and the cited account says what Lisbon did with it: paid for industrialised goods, textiles and weapons, from countries that had the industry Portugal lacked. The Methuen terms of 1703 had already guaranteed English textiles admission to Portugal at all times, whatever the political weather. What is disputed is the same thing that is disputed about Caribbean sugar — whether colonial windfalls of this kind financed British industrialisation or merely accompanied it — and the atlas will not settle from one side of it.
explanations.the-brazilian-gold-cycle--transfer-of-th: The reason given in the sources is logistical and is the whole of it: Rio de Janeiro lay closer to the mining region and gave the gold a harbour to leave from, so in 1763 the capital of the State of Brazil moved there from Salvador and the king’s representative began to be called Viceroy. The centre of gravity of the colony had already moved — by 1725 half the population lived in the south-east — and the capital followed it.

A court in flight goes somewhere that can keep it. The reason given for Brazil, in so many words, is that it was by then the richest and most developed of the Portuguese colonies, and what had made it so within living memory was the gold: eight hundred tonnes shipped over the century, half the population of the colony resettled into the south-east by 1725. The type is the weak one, and deliberately: the mines did not send the French army into Portugal. They are why the answer to the invasion could be a transatlantic capital rather than a surrender.
explanations.the-caribbean-sugar-revolution--royal-af: Twenty years after Drax brought the mill home, the restored Stuart crown chartered a company with a monopoly on all English trade with Africa, overseen by the king’s brother. It was chartered to look for gold on the Gambia and it went into people instead, and historians estimate it shipped more enslaved Africans to the Americas than any other company. The demand it turned to was the sugar islands’, and the turn is what the edge claims.
explanations.the-caribbean-sugar-revolution--the-atla: Sugar was a cash crop with economies of scale, grown most efficiently on large estates with many workers, and the sources say the plantations made extensive use of enslaved people for that reason. The proportions move together: three quarters of the islands European before 1650, three enslaved Africans to every planter after the cane. The causal claim is the strong one and is about magnitude — the traffic to the Caribbean existed before the sugar revolution and became the largest forced migration in history because of it.
explanations.wheeler-s-surprise--battle-of-bloody-bro: The Bloody Brook article makes the Brookfield siege the reason the militia were in the Connecticut valley at all: "In the aftermath of the Siege of Brookfield in the first few months of King Philip's War, the New England Confederation raised several companies of English militia and indigenous allies to protect the western border of the colony, as the settlements there were not able to conscript enough men for their defense." One of those companies is what was destroyed at Bloody Brook six weeks later. Precondition-of and not caused: the siege did not order the wagon train out, it put the companies in the valley. Wikipedia is the only author named, so probable.
